page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.i2ne.4xlarge is an x86_64 architecture server powered by an Intel Xeon 8163 processor running at 2.5 GHz. It features 16 dedicated vCPUs derived from 8 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The system is equipped with 128.0 GB of RAM, providing 8.0 GB of memory per core, and includes 3839 GB of local SSD storage. Network connectivity is supported by a 5 Gbps baseline bandwidth.

Benchmark results indicate a clear distinction between single-core and multi-core performance. Single-core metrics, such as stress-ng single-core and Geekbench single-core scores, fall into the bottom 25% tier, with single-threaded gzip compression rated as poor. However, multi-core performance is more robust, achieving average ratings in stress-ng multi-core, Passmark CPU, and Geekbench multi-core tests. Memory read-only bandwidth is average, though the Passmark memory score is positioned in the lower 25%.

Given the substantial 3839 GB of bundled local SSD storage and 128 GB of RAM, this server offers high resource density for storage-intensive applications. It is qualitatively cost-efficient for workloads that require large local scratch space or high-capacity caching without needing top-tier single-core compute speeds. The hardware profile is well-suited for database operations, Redis deployments, static web serving, and multi-threaded data processing tasks.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.i2ne.4xlarge is an x86_64 server powered by an Intel Xeon 8163 processor with 16 dedicated vCPUs and 128.0 GB of RAM. Performance benchmarks show weak single-core capabilities, but multi-core performance, memory bandwidth, and database operations consistently reach average tiers. This resource configuration, combining high-capacity local storage with a 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, provides a cost-effective profile for storage-heavy and memory-intensive workloads. It is highly suitable for database hosting, Redis caching layers, static web serving, and multi-threaded data processing where massive local storage is required but extreme single-core processing speed is not critical.
